title: Price Tracking Service
seoTitle: Design a Price Tracking Service Like CamelCamelCamel
description: Design a price tracker — collecting product prices at scale, showing price history charts, and notifying users when a price drops below their target.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Price Tracking Service?
blocks.text: A price tracker (like CamelCamelCamel or Honey) monitors product prices on e-commerce sites, shows how a price has changed over time, and alerts users when a product drops below a price they choose.

items: Users should be able to view the price history of a product as a chart.
Users should be able to subscribe to a price-drop alert with a target price.
Users should be notified (by email) when the price falls below their target.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Track ~500M products; popular products should be checked at least hourly.
Price-drop alerts should go out within an hour of the change.
Price history charts should load in < 500ms.
Prefer availability; history can be eventually consistent.

blocks.text: The system has a **write-heavy ingestion** side (collecting billions of price points) and a lightweight read side. We'll design collection, storage and alerting, then go deep on each.

items: **Product**: a retailer product (URL/ASIN, title, current price).
**Subscription**: a user's alert — productId, targetPrice, status.

blocks.text: 1) Users should be able to view price history
Price points are written by collectors and read by a **Product Service** that returns the series for a time range.
2) Users should be able to subscribe to price drops
A **Subscription Service** stores subscriptions keyed by `productId`, with an index so we can quickly find every subscriber of a given product.
3) Users should be notified when the price drops

When a collector records a new price that is lower than the previous one, it emits a `price_changed` event. A **Notification Worker** looks up subscriptions for that product with `targetPrice >= newPrice` and sends emails.
1) How do we collect prices for 500M products?

blocks.title: Crawl every product on a fixed schedule

approach.text: Scrape all 500M product pages every hour.

challenges.text: That's ~140k page fetches per second, most for products nobody watches. We'd be blocked by retailers and the cost would be enormous.

approach.text: Assign each product a crawl priority based on number of subscribers, views, and how volatile its price has been. A scheduler places products on a priority queue; popular items are checked hourly, the long tail daily or weekly.

challenges.text: Rarely viewed products may miss short-lived deals; that's an acceptable trade.

blocks.title: Prioritised crawling + official APIs + crowd-sourced prices

approach.text: Use retailer product APIs where available (cheaper and allowed), prioritised crawling elsewhere, and accept price observations from the browser extension when users visit product pages — validated against recent crawls to reject bad data.

challenges.text: Crowd-sourced data must be verified (e.g. require agreement or a confirming crawl before alerting) to avoid false notifications.

blocks.text: 2) How should we store billions of price points?

blocks.title: One relational table with a row per observation

challenges.text: Billions of rows grow without bound; range scans for a chart get slower and storage is wasteful when the price rarely changes.

blocks.title: Store changes only, in a time-series store

approach.text: Write a point **only when the price changes** (plus a periodic heartbeat), which shrinks data dramatically. Use a time-series database (e.g. TimescaleDB, or Cassandra partitioned by `productId` with clustering on `ts`). Chart queries are a single-partition range scan; pre-aggregate daily min/max for long periods.

challenges.text: A chart now needs "carry forward" logic between change points, which the client or service handles.

blocks.text: 3) How do we notify subscribers efficiently and reliably?

blocks.title: Query subscriptions on every price change

approach.text: On each `price_changed` event, `SELECT user_id FROM subscriptions WHERE product_id = ? AND target_price >= ? AND status = 'ACTIVE'`, then send emails.

challenges.text: Works well with an index on `(product_id, target_price)`. A popular product might have hundreds of thousands of subscribers, so sending must be batched.

blocks.title: Event-driven pipeline with a durable queue

approach.text: Collectors publish `price_changed` events to Kafka partitioned by `productId`. Notification workers fetch matching subscriptions, enqueue individual email jobs, and mark each subscription `NOTIFIED` (so a user isn't spammed if the price bounces). The email sender is idempotent per `(subscriptionId, priceEventId)`.

challenges.text: Must handle retries and deduplication carefully; that's what the idempotency key is for.

quiz.question: What is the most effective way to cut price-history storage?
options: Write a point only when the price changes
quiz.explanation: Prices change rarely, so recording only changes removes most redundant rows.

quiz.question: How should crawl frequency be decided?
options: By priority: subscribers, views and price volatility
quiz.explanation: Spending crawl budget where users care keeps alerts timely without crawling the long tail hourly.

quiz.question: Why mark a subscription as NOTIFIED after sending?
options: To avoid spamming users when the price fluctuates around the target
quiz.explanation: Without it, a price bouncing above and below the target would trigger repeated emails.

quiz.question: Which index best supports finding subscribers for a price change?
quiz.explanation: It lets the query jump directly to a product's subscriptions with target at or above the new price.
